newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Unanimity to remain in most sensistive areas.
newsitem.headline: Unanimity to remain in most sensistive areas.

text.p: The European Union has given up on plans for a sweeping move to Qualified Majority Voting, opting to retain unanimity in the most sensitive policy areas, according to a Dutch EU presidency document obtained by Reuters.

Drafted for a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Rome next Tuesday, the document says that IGC negotiators are now likely to limit their discussion of QMV mainly to issues related to the functioning of the single market.

"Broad agreement has emerged that provisions of a constitutional or quasi-constitutional nature...as well as those which have a direct impact on expenditure or revenue of member states' budgets should continue to be suject to unanimity," the document says.
It also lists provisions which constitute derogations to the internal market.
What is left to be negotiated in the inter-governmental conference (IGC), due to end in June, would be an extension of majority voting in relatively minor fields.
"It (would be) a very small, very modest increase," said one EU diplomat.
The question of doing away with unanimity has been one of the most controversial facing the IGC.
Britain's Conservative government has said it will block any move to do away with the veto, which is already limited, fearing a loss of sovereignty.
Most other countries believe majority voting is the only way for the bloc to be efficient as it expands its numbers with the planned enlargement into eastern Europe.
But on the most sensitive issues, it has been impossible for the EU members to agree on majority voting in sensitive areas even without Britain.
The apparent agreement to limit the extension of majority voting could lead to a reasonably rapid agreement among negotiators if Britain's Labour Party wins Britain's May 1 general election.
Robin Cook, the man who is likely to negotiate for Britain under a Labour government, has said his party would not follow the Conservative line of blocking any move to majority voting.
He said this month that Labour would not give up the veto in sensitive areas, but would look at all other areas on a case-by-case basis.
